title: Common Collections Algorithms
learningObjectives: Sort and reverse lists using the Collections utility algorithms
Find minimum and maximum values in a non-empty collection
Use binarySearch only when the list follows the same sorted order
Explain when collection algorithms mutate the supplied list

understand.concept: Collections provides algorithms for lists. Sorting changes a list in place; binarySearch requires the list to be sorted using the same ordering.
understand.whyItMatters: Common Collections Algorithms helps learners create Java applications that are easier to reason about, test and maintain.
understand.analogy: Treat the concept as a clearly labeled tool for one programming responsibility.
understand.analogyLimit: Actual behavior is defined by Java language rules and API contracts.

explain.narrative:
## Algorithms supplied by Collections

The `Collections` utility class provides static algorithms that operate on collections, especially Lists. Common operations include sort, reverse, shuffle, frequency, min, max, swap and binarySearch. Most of these methods operate on the supplied list rather than creating a new list.

## Sorting and searching

`Collections.sort(list)` sorts according to natural ordering; the overload accepting a Comparator uses the supplied ordering. `Collections.binarySearch(list, key)` requires the list to be sorted using the same ordering used by the search. If the key is absent, the result is a negative insertion-point encoding, not simply -1. Do not interpret a search result as a valid index unless it is non-negative.

## Reordering and counting

`reverse` reverses the current order, `shuffle` applies a random permutation, and `swap` exchanges two positions. `frequency` counts elements equal to a target. `min` and `max` find the least or greatest element according to natural ordering or a supplied Comparator. These methods need a non-empty collection for min/max; empty input causes NoSuchElementException.

## Mutability and algorithm requirements

An algorithm that modifies a list requires a list that supports the relevant mutation. Immutable lists such as those returned by `List.of` cannot be sorted or reversed in place and will throw UnsupportedOperationException. Make a mutable copy when mutation is required.

## Test exact assumptions

Use deterministic data for output examples. Test duplicates, empty lists, absent search keys, custom comparators and immutable inputs. For shuffle, verify membership and size rather than expecting a fixed order.

examples.title: Core API
examples.code: public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { java.util.List<Integer> values = new java.util.ArrayList<>(java.util.List.of(3,1,2)); java.util.Collections.sort(values); System.out.println(values); } }
examples.explanation: Collections.sort mutates this ArrayList into natural ascending order.

examples.title: Practical use
examples.code: public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { java.util.List<Integer> values = new java.util.ArrayList<>(java.util.List.of(1,2,3)); java.util.Collections.reverse(values); System.out.println(values); } }
examples.explanation: reverse changes the order of elements in the mutable list; it does not create a separately sorted list.

examples.title: Boundary behavior
examples.code: public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { java.util.List<Integer> values = java.util.List.of(1,2,2,3); System.out.println(java.util.Collections.frequency(values,2)); } }
examples.explanation: frequency counts elements equal to the requested target, so the value 2 occurs twice.

examples.title: Alternative pattern
examples.code: public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { java.util.List<Integer> values = java.util.List.of(1,2,3,4); System.out.println(java.util.Collections.binarySearch(values,3)); } }
examples.explanation: The list is already sorted in ascending order, and binarySearch returns the zero-based index where 3 is found.

examples.title: Verify the result
examples.code: public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { java.util.List<Integer> values = java.util.List.of(4,2,8); System.out.println(java.util.Collections.max(values)); } }
examples.explanation: max selects the greatest element according to natural ordering for this non-empty integer list.

practise.guidedTask: Sort a mutable list, reverse it, count a repeated value with frequency and find a value with binarySearch. Predict every output first.
practise.independentTask: Build a leaderboard that sorts scores, reports minimum and maximum, and counts how often a target score appears.
hints: Before binarySearch, sort with the same natural ordering or Comparator that the search will use.
Check whether the list supports mutation before calling sort, reverse, swap or shuffle; List.of returns an unmodifiable list.
For binarySearch, distinguish a non-negative found index from the negative insertion-point result; test empty and missing-key cases.
practise.challenge: Demonstrate why binarySearch can return an unexpected result on an unsorted list, then sort with the same Comparator and test again.

questions.prompt: What must be true before using Collections.binarySearch on a list?
options: The list must be sorted using the same ordering
The list must contain only strings
questions.answer: The list must be sorted using the same ordering
questions.explanation: binarySearch requires the list to be sorted using the same ordering as the search; otherwise the result is not reliable.

questions.prompt: Which Collections method reverses list order?
questions.explanation: Collections.reverse reverses the current encounter order of a mutable list.

questions.prompt: Which method counts occurrences of a value in a collection?
questions.explanation: Collections.frequency counts occurrences equal to the supplied target element.

questions.prompt: What does Collections.sort do to a mutable list?
options: Returns a new immutable list only
Converts the list to a Set
questions.explanation: Collections.sort sorts the supplied mutable list in place rather than returning a newly allocated sorted list.

questions.prompt: Which method chooses a random permutation of a list?
questions.explanation: Collections.shuffle randomizes the order of the elements while retaining the same elements.
